tokenization-embeddings.summary: Models read token ids from a learned subword vocabulary, not words or letters, which explains token counts, cost, multilingual fragmentation and letter-counting failures. Embeddings start as a lookup table, become contextual inside the transformer, and, after contrastive training, become sentence vectors whose similarity metric and normalisation you must handle correctly.
points: BPE starts from base symbols and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair, then applies merges in learned order at inference. Byte-level BPE (GPT-2, RoBERTa) starts from 256 bytes, so it never needs an unknown token; GPT-2's vocabulary is 50,257.

WordPiece (BERT, 30K vocabulary) scores pairs by freq(pair) / (freq(a) x freq(b)), marks word-internal pieces with `##`, and tokenises by longest match; an unmatched word becomes `[UNK]`. Unigram (T5, ALBERT, XLNet) starts large, prunes by loss, and picks the most probable segmentation with Viterbi.

The Hugging Face pipeline is normalization (Unicode, lowercase, accents), pre-tokenization (word-like splits; GPT-2 keeps spaces as `Ġ`, SentencePiece uses `▁` and is reversible), model, then post-processing (special tokens such as `[CLS] ... [SEP]`).

Token counts depend on the tokenizer. With GPT-2's tokenizer, `This is a test.` is 5 tokens while its Hindi equivalent is 27: Devanagari characters are 3 UTF-8 bytes each and get few merges in a mostly English vocabulary.
Numbers: GPT-2 chunks digits inconsistently (`123|45|678`); Llama 2 splits every number into individual digits and uses byte fallback for unknown characters. Leading spaces and case change token ids.

Larger vocabularies shorten sequences but add a d_model-sized row to the embedding and output matrices per entry (32K to 128K at d = 4096 adds about 786M parameters untied) and spread training signal over rarer tokens.

An embedding layer equals one-hot times a V x d matrix, implemented as an index lookup. Weight tying reuses that matrix for the output logits, saving V x d parameters (GPT-2 config ties by default); Press and Wolf showed it also lowers perplexity.

Chat models need their own template: role and end-of-turn control tokens. Use `apply_chat_template` with `add_generation_prompt=True`; if you render with `tokenize=False` then tokenise, pass `add_special_tokens=False` to avoid a duplicate BOS.

Static vectors (Word2Vec, GloVe) give one vector per word; transformer hidden states are contextual. Raw BERT CLS or mean vectors scored below averaged GloVe on STS in the SBERT paper, so use models trained for embeddings.

Sentence-embedding models are bi-encoders trained contrastively: `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss` (InfoNCE) uses other in-batch positives as negatives, and scale = 1 / temperature (default 20). Bigger batches give more negatives. A cross-encoder over all pairs of 10,000 sentences takes about 65 hours, a bi-encoder about 5 seconds.
Cosine ignores length; dot product rewards large norms; for unit vectors |a - b|^2 = 2 - 2cos, so dot, cosine and Euclidean rank identically. Use dot on normalised vectors because it is cheaper.

Matryoshka training makes leading dimensions usable on their own (up to 14x smaller at equal accuracy in the paper). Truncation saves storage and search cost, not forward-pass cost; renormalise after truncating.
traps: Tokens are not words, and characters / 4 is only an English rule of thumb; count with the target model's own tokenizer, including template tokens.
Letter counting and string reversal fail because the model sees token ids; route character-level work to code.
Adding tokens and calling `resize_token_embeddings` gives untrained rows; the model needs training on the new language before they help.
Setting pad = EOS and masking labels by pad id also masks the real EOS, so the model never learns to stop.
Vectors from different embedding models (or versions) are not comparable; switching models means re-embedding the corpus.
Mined hard negatives are often unlabelled positives; false negatives teach the model to push correct answers away.
